prize_parts.citation: For a poetic, essayistic and translational oeuvre that renews lyric and narrative form through a sustained encounter with classical antiquity, grief and desire.

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading the colleagues' arguments. Carson's claim rests on distinctiveness of voice, formal invention and intellectual depth. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon material as a verse novel. Nox turns an elegy for her brother into a book-object built from a Catullus translation, archival fragments and commentary. Her versions of Greek texts show that her scholarship is part of her poetic practice and not a separate activity. That unity of philological rigour and lyric risk is difficult to mistake for anyone else's work. The oeuvre has spanned decades and kept finding new forms, so the formal radicalism looks like sustained development and not a single gesture. Among the shortlisted candidates, I think hers best combines linguistic and formal achievement with emotional and intellectual weight. Cărtărescu and Adonis are the strongest alternatives on the same criteria, and I keep them as such.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the hybrid and book-object works do not reduce to text. A committee reading in translation, and ordinary editions, may not capture what Nox or the other design-dependent books do. The corpus mixes original poems, translations, adaptations and essays, so judging 'sustained quality' and 'significance across the body of work' involves interpretation. It is also fair to ask whether concentrated, erudite and formally radical work carries the idealistic weight of Nobel's will as fully as Cărtărescu's large imaginative project or Adonis's remaking of a poetic language.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg values Carson's unmistakable voice and the emotional power of Nox, but asks how much of the oeuvre is original creation as against translation and adaptation, and whether the formal play is sometimes mannered.
responses.response: I take the question seriously, and a citation must be drawn with care. My view is that in her case translation and adaptation are not a separate category. Her renderings of Greek texts and her original verse and essays share one voice and one method, and Nox is itself a translation turned into an original elegy. I would credit the whole practice and not claim the translations as independent creation. The risk of mannerism is real in some of the more occasional later work. I cannot settle it from general public knowledge, and it remains open. I regard it as a qualification of the case and not a refutation.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for voice, imaginative depth and sustained ambition across novels, poetry and essays, while acknowledging that she cannot assess the Romanian sentence-level texture in translation.
responses.response: I agree that Cărtărescu's imaginative scale and voice are exceptional, and I ranked him second for that reason. The translation caveat applies to both of us and to him in particular, because his achievement lies in the density and rhythm of Romanian prose. That makes the weakest point in his case the same as in Carson's, which is translation dependence, but I would argue Carson's formal inventiveness is more verifiable through her English text. I still hold that the long digressive structures raise a question of economy that Carson's concentration avoids. I would not dismiss his case, and I keep him as an alternative.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first but notes that her corpus is smaller and more fragmentary than that of many novelists, so the committee must decide how much weight to give concentrated, formally radical work over bulk.
responses.response: That is the right question, and I would answer that volume is not a criterion in itself. What matters is whether the achievement is sustained and significant across the body of work. Carson's books over several decades show continued formal development, not repetition, and the fragment as a poetic form is itself part of the achievement. I still accept that the committee should test this claim against the late work and not rely on the canonical books alone.

responses.point: Palm, who also ranks Carson first, is uncertain whether the hybrid, scholarly mode would be read as literature of the broad ideal significance that Nobel's will describes.
responses.response: I think the will's 'ideal direction' should not be read as excluding learned or experimental work, and the Academy's practice has not required that. The better test is whether the work gives imaginative and human depth to its formal invention. In Nox and Autobiography of Red, grief, desire and the relation to the dead carry the formal play, which supports her case. I accept that this is a matter of judgement on which colleagues may reasonably differ.

uncertainties: Many of Carson's books depend on typography, visual and material design, which translation and standard editions may not reproduce, so a text-based assessment is partial.
I rely on general public knowledge and have not independently verified sources or read the full corpus. Whether the later output keeps the level of the earlier major books is unconfirmed.
The boundary between original work, translation and adaptation in a citation is a matter of interpretation.
For Cărtărescu and Adonis, my reading depends on translation and cannot judge the Romanian prose or the Arabic prosody directly, so any comparison among the three remains provisional.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile that would require recusal. For context only, my scholarly interests in the literary fragment, translation and exile literature overlap thematically with parts of Carson's practice. This is not evidence of a preference and I do not treat it as a conflict.
